Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Leilani was six years old the first time she saw her mother’s face change—the way it crumpled, then went still, as if the woman who sang lullabies had been replaced by someone else. Her father’s voice would rise through the thin walls of their Honolulu apartment, a shape she learned to recognize before the words even landed. She would press herself into the corner of her room, counting the seconds until the door slammed, until her mother came to find her with a practiced smile. That was how it went for years: the yelling, the crashing, the silence afterward. She never spoke of it. By the time she was ten, Leilani had learned to make herself small, to watch without being seen, to disappear into the rhythm of her own heartbeat.

As an adult, she became a dancer—a profession that demanded exactly the kind of visibility she had spent her childhood avoiding. On stage, under the lights, she could transform into something else, a body in motion that belonged to the music, not to the past. But the control she felt in choreographed movement began to fray after she married. Her husband’s name is David. She loves him, but she cannot bear to hear his name spoken by others. Whenever a coworker says “David” in casual conversation, her chest tightens. She once asked her closest friend to call him “your husband” instead. The explanation she gave was that it felt more intimate. In truth, she did not know why it terrified her—only that it did.

The worst moments come without warning. She will be stretching before rehearsal, her heart rate rising from exertion, and suddenly the pounding in her ears becomes the pounding of fists, the slam of a door, the voice she used to pray would stop. Her mind is back in that corner, but her body is here—on a dance floor, surrounded by mirrors. And every mirror reflects her, and every reflection is watched. The feeling of being observed, even when she is alone, has become a constant hum. She scans rooms for eyes. She avoids the front edge of the stage. She has started to arrive late to class and leave early, slipping out before the applause.

There are other times when she can recall the event—the screams, the objects breaking, the way her mother’s hand shook afterward—but she feels nothing. A hollow numbness spreads through her chest, as though the memory belongs to a stranger. She tells herself it was not that bad, that others had it worse, that she is overreacting. But then, without any trigger she can name, the full weight of it crashes into her again, and she is crying in the dressing room, not knowing why.

Leilani has come to believe that she was betrayed by someone she trusted—her father, yes, but also her mother, who stayed, who smiled, who told her everything was fine. And if that could happen, if the people closest to you could be something other than what they seemed, then how could she trust anyone? She has never said this aloud, but she is certain that there is something about her that made the event happen. A flaw. A wrongness. She does not know what it is, only that it must be there, because why else would she have been the one to see it, to carry it, to feel it still?

For months, her husband has noticed her pulling away. She flinches when he touches her unexpectedly. She has stopped inviting him to performances. At her last company review, the director pulled her aside and said she seemed “distracted,” that her artistry was fading. Leilani wanted to explain that she was fighting a war in her head, but she could not find the words. She finally sought help after a matinee performance last week. The audience was small. A man in the second row had the same name as her father. She heard someone say it during intermission—just a name, nothing more—and she could not go back on stage. She stood in the wings, heart pounding, and watched the music play without her.

What frightens her most is not the memory itself, but the belief that she is broken in a way that cannot be fixed. She wants to go back to the person who could dance without thinking. She is not sure that person still exists. But she is here, in the chair across from the therapist, and she is willing to try.
